amendments.why: Rule 46 already gives a recast Hebrew noun its supplied relative (`מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest*), but that sentence sits inside the headless-relative paragraph, and the rider following it states the boundary only from the finite-clause side. Read alone, that rider and rule 55's *do not fold it into the verb* push a verse pass toward `added` whenever a written noun stands before the English relative, which is what happened at JOS.4.3: the same recasting the chapter gave to `מַצָּב` at JOS.4.9 and to `מָלוֹן` at JOS.4.8 was marked a surplus there. The amendment states the boundary from the nominal side and gives the subtraction test, narrowing nothing and preserving the Numbers rider whole. It also settles the companion question this chapter met: a lexical English verb standing inside such a recasting (*lodged*, *stood*) is what the noun's own lexeme names, so rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause does not reach it either. Three units in one chapter carry the pattern, and rule 46's own `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` example is the precedent.
amendments.rule: **An anarthrous substantive takes the English the ASV supplies to make it one.** A participle or adjective used as a noun with no article morpheme present still needs an English noun phrase, and the ASV supplies it: a bare *the*, or a pronoun with a relative — *him that*, *them that*, *they that*, *those that*. No article is present to take that English and nothing else licenses it, so it joins the substantive's own unit and is never `added`. `זֵדִים` → *the proud*, `צַדִּיק` → *the righteous*, `יִרְאֵי יְהֵוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah*, `עֹשְׁקֵי` → *those that oppress*, `עֹבֵד` → *him that serveth*. **Head on the word carrying the lexeme**, by rule 31's subtraction: *proud*, *righteous*, *feared*, *oppress*, *serveth*. This does not contradict rule 41's heading on the pronoun. There the supplied pronoun is the whole of what the article is rendered by, so it is the only candidate; here the substantive's own lexeme sits in the same unit and outranks a word the ASV supplied. Read whether an article morpheme is present, and let that decide which rule governs. Two riders. Where the Hebrew supplies a relative of its own, that relative takes the *that* and the supplied antecedent goes with it — `לַאֲשֶׁר לֹא עֲבָדוֹ` → *him that serveth him not* puts *him that* on `אֲשֶׁר` — since a present morpheme takes its English before a bare participle does. And where the ASV writes the antecedent once across coordinated substantives, the later ones take only what is written: `וְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ` → *and that thought upon his name* leaves the participle *that thought upon*, under rule 22. **A headless relative clause is read the same way, and its verb may be finite.** Where the Hebrew writes a relative clause with no antecedent noun and no `אֲשֶׁר`, the whole clause stands in a nominal slot and the ASV must supply a noun phrase for it: `אַחֲרֵי לֹא יוֹעִילוּ הָלָכוּ` → *walked after* ***things that do*** *not* ***profit***, `בְלוֹא יוֹעִיל` → *for* ***that which doth*** *not* ***profit***. The supplied antecedent and relative join the clause's own unit and head on the word carrying the lexeme, exactly as *them that* joins a bare participle above and for the same reason: no article and no relative morpheme is present to take them, and nothing else licenses them, so neither is `added`. The unit is discontinuous around the negative or any other intervening word under rule 25, and a Hebrew noun the ASV recasts the same way — `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* — goes with it. **This governs only a clause with no antecedent of its own.** Where the Hebrew writes the antecedent and the ASV supplies a relative for a finite clause juxtaposed to it, nothing in this rule licenses that word: it subordinates a clause rather than making one a noun, and rules 30 and 55 are what decide it. **And a substantive the Hebrew writes is such an antecedent, whatever English this rule supplied to make it one.** An anarthrous participle or adjective for which the ASV has written *him that*, *they that* or *He who* is a written antecedent exactly as a common noun is, so a further relative the ASV writes over a finite clause juxtaposed to it answers to no morpheme and is `added` under rule 55: `נְאֻם שֹׁמֵעַ אִמְרֵי אֵל ... מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → *He saith who heareth the words of God ...* ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* leaves that *Who* `added`, while the same clause written with a relative of its own — `אֲשֶׁר מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* — gives the word to the `אֲשֶׁר` under this rule's first rider. Do not read the supplied noun phrase as evidence that what follows is headless: ask whether a substantive stands before the clause, not whether that substantive's own English was written or supplied. Read what the ASV supplied, too, since the headless case writes an antecedent and a relative together — *things that*, *that which* — while a bare relative with no antecedent beside it subordinates a clause to what precedes and is rule 55's. Rule 41's articleless attributive is a third case again, and is decided there. **But those two sentences govern a clause the Hebrew writes, and no more.** Where instead the ASV recasts one Hebrew nominal — the noun together with whatever construct dependents it governs — as an English head noun and a relative clause, and no clause stands in the Hebrew for that relative to subordinate, the relative is part of the noun's own recasting: it joins that noun's unit and is never `added`, exactly as `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* is above. `מִמַּצַּב רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים` → *out of the place* ***where*** *the priests' feet stood firm* gives *the place where* to `מַצָּב`, and `אֶל־הַמָּלוֹן` → *unto the place* ***where*** *they lodged* gives the whole phrase to `מָלוֹן`. Head on the word carrying the noun's lexeme under rule 31, which is the English verb where the recasting writes one for it and the head noun where a written Hebrew verb already holds the predicate. **A lexical English verb standing inside such a recasting is not rule 20's supplied lexical verb either**, where that verb is what the noun's own lexeme names — a lodging place is where one lodges and a standing place where one stands — since dropping it leaves that noun's rendering short rather than removing a predication the Hebrew never wrote. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the English relative and ask whether the noun's own rendering is left incomplete, or whether a clause the Hebrew wrote has merely lost a subordinator. Where a Hebrew relative or resumptive morpheme does stand in the phrase it takes the English first, under this rule's first rider and rule 22, and the noun keeps only its own words: `בַּמָּלוֹן אֲשֶׁר תָּלִינוּ בוֹ` → *in the lodging place* ***where*** *ye shall lodge* leaves `מָלוֹן` the bare *lodging place*.

conventions: The doubled distributive `אִישׁ אֶחָד אִישׁ אֶחָד מִשָּׁבֶט` (JOS.4.2, JOS.4.4), rendered *out of every tribe a man*, gives the distributive *every* to the second `אֶחָד` under rule 41 and *a man* with its indefinite article to the first `אִישׁ` under rule 15, leaving the remaining `אֶחָד` and `אִישׁ` `unrepresented` under rule 22. The chapter takes the pairs in that order in both verses; the mirror allocation is equally available and is named in each verse's note.

In the catechetical formula `מָה הָאֲבָנִים הָאֵלֶּה` → *What mean these stones* (JOS.4.6, JOS.4.21) the *mean* is its own `added` unit and `מָה` keeps only *What*. It is not rule 20's construction-supplied copula: that rule's own example writes *is* (*What man is this*), while *mean* predicates meaning of the stones and is the supplied lexical verb rule 20 expressly leaves `added`. The `לְ` of `לָכֶם` still takes the *by* the ASV writes in JOS.4.6, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied-word analysis does.

`תַּמּוּ … לַעֲבוֹר` → *were clean passed over* (JOS.4.1, JOS.4.11) puts the adverb *clean* on the finite `תָּמַם` and the whole *were passed over* on the infinitive construct, discontinuous around it under rule 25, with the `לְ` `unrepresented` because the ASV writes no function word for it. The competing reading — *were clean* as the finite verb's own rendering — is named in both verses.

`לִפְנֵי` fuses whole even where the ASV spends four English words on it — `לִפְנֵי הָעָם` → *in the presence of the people* (JOS.4.11) — because no part of that compound is the `לְ`'s own relation, and rule 30 reads its condition as one rendering rather than one token. `בְּעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל` → *in the sight of all Israel* (JOS.4.14) splits instead, because the `בְּ`'s own locative sense is what the written *in* renders and the *of* is the chain's relation on the rectum. Read whether the English preposition states the Hebrew preposition's own relation before fusing or splitting.

report: One real cross-verse split: the English relative in a recast place-noun. JOS.4.9 gives the *where* of `תַּחַת מַצַּב רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים` → *in the place where … stood* to `מַצָּב`, and JOS.4.8 gives the whole *the place where they lodged* to `מָלוֹן`, but JOS.4.3 marked the *where* of `מִמַּצַּב רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים` → *out of the place where the priests feet stood firm* `added` under rule 55. All three recast a Hebrew nominal in which no clause stands for a relative to subordinate, so nothing in the source licenses the difference. The lemma table could not show it: an `added` unit has no source token and appears in no group.

The direction of the fix is determined rather than chosen. JOS.4.9 writes no verb morpheme at all, so *where … stood* can only be the noun's there; JOS.4.3 is what moves. `מַצָּב` now takes *the place where*, headed on *place*, and `הָכִין` keeps *stood firm* unchanged, headed on *firm*, with its competing reading still named. The chapter's `added` count falls from 4 to 3.

Checked and rejected as splits, each licensed by the source: `מִפְּנֵי` fused to *before* (4.7) beside the same pair split as *from before* (4.23), which is rule 30's own ruling; `לִפְנֵי` fused whole to *in the presence of* (4.11) beside `בְּעֵינֵי` split as *in* + *the sight* (4.14), since the `בְּ` has its own *in* written for it while no part of that four-word compound is the `לְ`'s own relation; `מָלוֹן` as *lodging place* in 4.3, where the Hebrew writes its own relative and resumptive suffix, against the full clause in 4.8, where it writes neither; `רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים` as an English possessive (4.3, 4.18) against an of-phrase (4.9), which rule 29 places by which determiner stands before the rectum's word.

Checked as already internally consistent: the doubled `אִישׁ אֶחָד אִישׁ אֶחָד`, distributed identically in 4.2 and 4.4; the three presentative `הָיָה` frames (4.1, 4.11, 4.18), each handing the frame's *that* to the apodosis waw; the two `מָה הָאֲבָנִים הָאֵלֶּה` formulas (4.6, 4.21), both leaving the supplied *mean* `added`; `כָּל־הַדָּבָר` → *everything* (4.10) and `כָּל־הַיָּמִים` → *for ever* (4.24), both fusing with the article `unrepresented` as rule 30's `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` ruling directs; and the demonstrative phrases of 4.6, 4.7, 4.9, 4.14, 4.20, 4.21 and 4.22, where the one written determiner is the demonstrative's and both articles go unrepresented.

BSB: every disagreement is a documented convention difference — articles (17), object markers (4), prepositions (7, mostly the `לְ` of `לֵאמֹר` and ethical datives), the paragogic nun, the surplus `אִישׁ` and `אֶחָד` of the doubled distributive, the `אַחַת` of 4.5 where the ASV writes only *a stone*, and the `בְּ` of 4.7 whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object. None is a genuine error, and nothing was changed to move the rate.

The 3-source-morpheme unit flagged in JOS.4.3 (`אֲשֶׁר` + `בְּ` + suffix → *where*) is rule 22's `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` fusion: the suffix is masculine singular and denotes `מָלוֹן`, the antecedent the relative modifies, so the resumption is inside the one English word. It stands.
